title: Smooth affine normal quotients and affine subgroup inverse images
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Group schemes and homomorphisms are as in [def-sc-group-scheme], closed and normal subgroup schemes as in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], smoothness as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme], and finite type as in [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-proper-morphism]. Affine means isomorphic to the spectrum of a commutative ring [def-pc-scheme]. Let $G$ be smooth, connected, separated and of finite type over $k$, and let $N\hookrightarrow G$ be a smooth connected affine closed normal subgroup scheme. There exist a smooth connected separated finite-type $k$-group scheme $Q$ and a smooth surjective homomorphism $q:G\to Q$ of finite presentation such that $N\hookrightarrow G$ is its scheme-theoretic kernel. For every $k$-scheme $T\to Q$, the projection $G\times_Q T\to T$ is flat, surjective and of finite presentation, hence a one-member covering in the big fppf topology [def-pc-fppf-site]. For every smooth connected affine closed normal subgroup scheme $S\hookrightarrow Q$, its inverse image $P=G\times_Q S$ [def-pc-fibre-product] is a smooth connected affine closed normal subgroup scheme of $G$ containing $N$, and $q|_P:P\to S$ is surjective and has scheme-theoretic kernel $N$. Finite presentation means locally of finite presentation [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation], quasi-compact and quasi-separated [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]; flatness is as in [def-weil-flat-morphism]. Neither $G$ nor $Q$ is assumed affine or commutative.

source.place: Theorem 5.14, printed p.102 and proof on p.105; Propositions 5.24--5.25 and Corollary 5.26, printed pp.104--105; Proposition 1.62 and its proof, printed p.24; Theorem 5.55 and Proposition 5.59, printed pp.113--114; Proposition 8.1(a), printed p.149. These give quotient, smoothness, subgroup correspondence and preservation of affineness/smoothness/connectedness under extension. The covering clause is base change of the smooth surjective quotient. No Stacks tag states the combined group-scheme assertion.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homogeneous-quotient] to the closed subgroup $N\hookrightarrow G$. It gives a separated finite-type scheme $Q$ and a flat surjective finitely presented map $q:G\to Q$ with $q(a)=q(b)$ exactly when $a^{-1}b\in N(U)$ for every test scheme $U$. As the subgroup inclusion is injective on points, the element $n$ with $b=an$ is unique. Hence $(a,n)\mapsto(a,an)$ is a natural bijection $G(U)\times N(U)\to(G\times_QG)(U)$ and, by [lem-galois-yoneda-fully-faithful], represents an isomorphism $\theta:G\times_kN\simeq G\times_QG$. The one-member family $\{q\}$ is an fpqc covering [def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering]: over an affine open $V\subset Q$, quasi-compactness of $q$ supplies finitely many affine opens covering $q^{-1}(V)$, and their images cover $V$ by surjectivity.

source.place: Theorem 5.28, Definition 5.20 and Propositions 5.24--5.25, printed pp.104--105

proof.text: For any $k$-scheme $T$, put $q_T=q\times\mathrm{id}_T:G\times_kT\to Q\times_kT$. It is an fpqc covering by [lem-galois-fpqc-covering-base-change]. Its kernel pair is $(G\times_QG)\times_kT$, identified by $\theta$ with $G\times_kN\times_kT$, with projections $(g,n,t)\mapsto(g,t)$ and $(g,n,t)\mapsto(gn,t)$. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] says precisely that a morphism $a:G\times_kT\to Y$ descends uniquely through $q_T$ if $a(gn,t)=a(g,t)$. In particular precomposition with $q_T$ is injective on morphisms. For $k$-morphisms the descended map is over $k$: its structure-map equality can be checked after $q_T$ by that same injectivity. Repeating this injectivity one variable at a time shows that morphisms out of $Q^r\times_kT$ agree if they agree after $q^r\times\mathrm{id}_T$.

source.place: Tag 023Q, lemma-fpqc-universal-effective-epimorphisms; parameterwise form of Milne Proposition 5.21

proof.text:
Construct multiplication on $Q$. Normality [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] gives $g_2^{-1}n_1g_2\in N(U)$ and hence
$$q((g_1n_1)(g_2n_2))=q(g_1g_2(g_2^{-1}n_1g_2)n_2)=q(g_1g_2).$$
This calculation holds on affine test schemes by the definition of normality, and on every test scheme by restriction to affine opens. First apply step 2 with parameter $G$ to descend $(g_1,g_2)\mapsto q(g_1g_2)$ in its first variable, giving $b:Q\times_kG\to Q$. The equality $b(x,g_2n_2)=b(x,g_2)$ can be checked after $q\times\mathrm{id}_{G\times N}$; there it is the displayed calculation. Descend again in the second variable (interchanging the factors in step 2). This gives $m_Q:Q\times_kQ\to Q$ with $m_Q(q(g_1),q(g_2))=q(g_1g_2)$.

source.place: Proposition 5.12 and proof of Theorem 5.14 after Theorem 5.28, printed pp.101,105

proof.text: The inverse descends because $(gn)^{-1}=g^{-1}(gn^{-1}g^{-1})$ and $gn^{-1}g^{-1}\in N(U)$, so $q((gn)^{-1})=q(g^{-1})$. Define $v_Q$ by step 2 and put $e_Q=q\circ e_G$. The two associativity maps out of $Q^3$ agree after $q^3$, since their values are $q((g_1g_2)g_3)$ and $q(g_1(g_2g_3))$. The left and right unit maps agree with the identity after $q$, since $q(eg)=q(g)=q(ge)$. The left and right inverse identities likewise follow after $q$ from $q(g^{-1}g)=q(e)=q(gg^{-1})$. The injectivity proved in step 2 makes these equalities hold on $Q$. Thus these maps give a group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme], and the defining identity for $m_Q$ makes $q$ a homomorphism. No commutativity is used.

source.place: Proposition 5.12 and proof of Theorem 5.14, printed pp.101,105

proof.text: For every test scheme $U$, step 1 with $a=e_G$ gives $q(g)=e_Q$ if and only if $g=i(n)$ for a unique $n\in N(U)$, where $i:N\hookrightarrow G$ is the given inclusion. By [def-pc-fibre-product] these are exactly the $U$-points of $G\times_{Q,q,e_Q}\operatorname{Spec}k$. The bijections are natural, so [lem-galois-yoneda-fully-faithful] identifies $i$ with the scheme-theoretic kernel inclusion. In particular $q\circ i=e_Q$.

Base change $q$ along itself. Under the factor swap of $G\times_QG$, this base change $G\times_QG\to G$ is identified with the projection to the first factor, which becomes $G\times_kN\to G$ under $\theta$. Since $N$ is affine, its structure map to $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is affine by [pqf-def-affine-morphism]; its base change is affine by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence](1). Since $N$ is smooth, the same projection is smooth by [lem-pc-proper-base-change](2). Apply [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-descend-affine] and [lem-trf-smooth-fpqc-base-descent] to the fpqc covering $q:G\to Q$ of step 1. They show that $q$ itself is affine and smooth. The hypotheses for smooth descent are flatness, quasi-compactness and surjectivity of $q$, all already supplied in step 1.

source.place: Tags 02L5 (lemma-descending-property-affine) and 02VL (lemma-descending-property-smooth); Milne Proposition 1.62(a), printed p.24, and Proposition 8.1(a), printed p.149

proof.text: Apply [lem-sbc-smooth-flat-surjective-source-descent] to $G\xrightarrow{q}Q\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. The map $q$ is flat, surjective and locally of finite presentation by step 1, and the composite is smooth by the hypothesis on $G$. Thus $Q$ is smooth. It is nonempty because $e_Q$ is a $k$-point, and it is connected: a partition of $Q$ into two disjoint nonempty opens would pull back by the continuous surjection $q$ to such a partition of $G$, contradicting its connectedness [def-weil-connected-scheme]. Its separatedness and finite type were already obtained in step 1.

source.place: Corollary 5.26 and Proposition 5.59(b), printed pp.105,114; smooth source descent as in Stacks Tag 05B5

proof.text: For any $T\to Q$, write $q_T:G\times_QT\to T$ for the base change. It is flat by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-morphism-base-change], surjective by [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-base-change], and of finite presentation by [lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-morphism-permanence](3). Hence $\{q_T\}$ is a covering of the big fppf site by the defining flat, locally finitely presented and jointly surjective condition of [def-pc-fppf-site]. This applies to arbitrary $T$, including nonreduced or non-quasi-compact $T$.

Let $S\hookrightarrow Q$ be as in the statement and set $P=G\times_QS$. The map $P\to G$ is a closed immersion by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-base-change]. On every affine test scheme $U$, its image is $\{g\in G(U):q(g)\in S(U)\}$, a subgroup because $q$ is a homomorphism. Multiplication, inverse and unit therefore restrict to $P$ by the fibre-product universal property. Moreover, for $a\in G(U)$ and $p\in P(U)$, $q(apa^{-1})=q(a)q(p)q(a)^{-1}\in S(U)$ by normality of $S$. Thus $P$ is a closed normal subgroup scheme by [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. The homomorphism $q|_P:P\to S$ is the pullback projection. Its kernel is $P\times_S\operatorname{Spec}k\simeq G\times_Q\operatorname{Spec}k=N$ by pullback pasting [def-pc-fibre-product] and step 5; this also gives the inclusion $N\subseteq P$. Its surjectivity and flatness follow from step 8 with $T=S$.

By step 6 and [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence](1), $P\to S$ is affine. Since $S$ is affine, clause (2) of that same node gives that $P$ is affine. Also $P$ is of finite type over $k$: its closed immersion into $G$ is proper by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fp-permanence](c), hence of finite type by [def-weil-proper-morphism], and its composite with $G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is of finite type by [lem-sfb-finite-type-composition-base-change](1). This establishes the finite-type hypotheses needed for the affine group-extension result below.

source.place: Proposition 8.1(a), printed p.149, affineness clause via affine descent; Stacks Tags 01W5 and 01T3 for finite type

proof.text: The map $P\to S$ is smooth by base change of the smooth map $q$ [lem-pc-proper-base-change](2). Since $S\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth by hypothesis, [lem-trf-smooth-composition] implies that $P\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth. Finally apply [lem-sfb-connected-group-extension] to $P\to S$. Both groups are affine of finite type: $P$ by step 10, and $S$ because it is affine, hence quasi-compact, and smooth, hence locally of finite presentation [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], so locally of finite type, since a finitely presented algebra is finitely generated [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]; the homomorphism is flat and surjective by step 8, and its scheme-theoretic kernel is $N$ by step 9. Both $N$ and $S$ are connected by hypothesis, so $P$ is connected. Together with steps 9--10 this proves every assertion about the inverse image, including its scheme-theoretic kernel and surjective restriction.
